In case of paywall:

There's a fatso I'd like you to meet, a real slob who readily says hello to the next pizza and to hell with personal restraint. He chugs down beer, likes a smoke, prefers two meat pies for lunch, biscuits with his frequent coffees and then a massive carb-loaded dinner, preferably with a plate that, when emptied, is filled with oily stuff that can be soaked up with a large slab of bread. Buttered, of course.

Hey, fat boy. Get up from that table and give us a look at that billowing second chin, that wobbly thing dangling close to breasts a supermodel would envy and just above a stomach suggesting twins might be on the way, if it were not for that crumb-laden moustache above your lip.

Obesity is a growing problem around the world. Obesity is a growing problem around the world. Photo: Stocksy I'd like to introduce everyone to ... me. A little more than three decades ago. Young bloke no longer playing sport, living alone in a small flat in a big city not too far from a strip of fast food joints and pubs. Wasn't hard to take a previously skinny kid and inflate him to almost 115 kilograms.

What proved harder was deflating him. After headaches, rising blood pressure and a blunt doctor who wondered aloud if I wanted to make it to 30, I started on a self-devised diet and exercise program that would take months to carve off almost 25 kilograms of blubber.

The author in heavier (and more hirsute days). The author in heavier (and more hirsute days). It wasn't simple. But fear of dying early is a startling motivational tool. Even now there's a fat guy lurking inside me desperate to embark on another calorific orgy. But I do my best to keep him restrained and hidden from view, if only because everyone hates being around someone who constantly burps and farts.

Yet I see reflections of him all around me. Large reflections. Australia, along with the rest of the developed world, is in the grip of an obesity pandemic, with more than one in five Australians considered seriously overweight. Just this week the New England Journal of Medicine told us that 100 million children and 600 million adults around the world were now obese, and that obesity rates had doubled in more than 70 countries since 1980. All up, almost a third of the planet's population is either overweight or officially obese.

But whereas 30 years ago it was my fault that I was overweight, these days a fleshy finger is being pointed elsewhere. Cottage industries have sprung up demanding doctors stop using terms like overweight and obese because they are discriminatory and do nothing but "shame" individuals. And the reasons that these individuals are way "larger" than mountains of medical evidence suggests they should be?

Why, any self-pitying lard-arse can readily produce a list of evil-doers who have forced them to stand for hours in front of an open fridge or pantry. There's the evil multinational food companies, secretly force-feeding us processed slop for decades. There are the pedlars of sugar, holding us captive and pouring copious amounts of that poisonous white substance down our mouths. And let's not forget those recently discovered genes showing many of us are predisposed to helping ourselves to a second and third helping of our preferred comfort food.

In other words, it ain't your fault. In Britain, which will introduce a sugar tax next year, there is a push to reduce portion sizes, particularly when it comes to packaged frozen meals. Because people, apparently, just can't help themselves and require the intervention of government. In NSW, the health department is now running nonsensical commercials - at our expense - telling parents that it's ... umm ... errr ... wise to encourage the kids to go outside and play and exercise. Because we didn't know that already.

We've now been living for decades in a previously unimaginable world with unlimited knowledge a swipe or click away. If people plead ignorance that stuffing more food into their mouths and doing less exercise leads to weight gain, then what hope?

If we as a society believe we have the right to intervene - if only to prevent health costs from also ballooning - then we should get serious and do what we did to smokers decades ago. They paid for their nicotine addiction. So isn't it time we got serious and brought in a fat tax? And not just on sugary drinks. How about hiking the price of chips and takeaway food while increasing insurance premiums and the cost of medical visits for those refusing to undertake serious weight loss programs?

But let's start by stopping those obesity apologists from hijacking a public policy debate and turning it into an argument over hurting someone's feelings. This is all about health. So let's utter that powerful four-letter word that once made even me flinch.

Come on. Say it after me. Diet.
